meta.source: World Economic Forum, The Future of Jobs Report 2025 (published January 2025). Survey of over 1,000 employers across 22 industry clusters and 55 economies, projecting 2025 to 2030.
meta.status: DRAFT SLICE. Written from recollection of the report because the WEF site was unreachable from the build environment. Every entry carries verified:false until checked against the PDF. Do not demo until checked.
meta.howToVerify: Open the PDF. For each entry, find the figure or section named in ref, confirm the wording and any number, then set verified:true and checkedOn.
meta.licensingNote: Confirm WEF terms of use for citing the report inside a product. Attribution is expected.

headline.claim: Employers expect 170 million jobs to be created by 2030.
headline.ref: Section 2, Total job growth and loss

headline.claim: Employers expect 92 million jobs to be displaced by 2030.
headline.ref: Section 2, Total job growth and loss

headline.claim: Net growth of 78 million jobs, about 7 percent of current employment.
headline.ref: Section 2, Total job growth and loss

headline.claim: Structural labour market churn of about 22 percent of jobs by 2030.
headline.ref: Section 2, Total job growth and loss

headline.claim: On average, 39 percent of workers' existing skill sets will be transformed or become outdated by 2030.
63 percent of employers identify skills gaps as the biggest barrier to business transformation.
85 percent of employers plan to prioritise upskilling their workforce.
About 70 percent of employers plan to hire staff with new AI skills; about 40 percent plan to reduce staff where AI can automate tasks.
In 2025 employers estimate tasks are done 47 percent by humans, 22 percent by technology, 30 percent by a combination.
By 2030 employers expect roughly a third each: human, technology, and combination.

drivers.label: Broadening digital access
drivers.ref: Section 1, Drivers of labour market transformation

drivers.label: Rising cost of living and slower growth
Ageing and declining working-age populations (high-income economies)

skills.label: Analytical thinking
skills.ref: Section 3, Core skills in 2025; Skills on the rise

taskCategories.label: Information and data processing
taskCategories.note: Reporting, data entry, reconciliation, collation. The category the report and its respondents expect to shift most to technology.
taskCategories.ref: Section 3, Automation and augmentation; derived category

taskCategories.label: Routine administration and scheduling
taskCategories.note: Diary, rota, inbox triage, form filling. Sits behind the decline in administrative assistant and clerk roles.

taskCategories.label: Written communication and drafting
taskCategories.note: First drafts, summaries, replies. Generative AI's strongest area is text; judgment and voice stay with the person.

taskCategories.label: Analysis and decision support
taskCategories.note: Analytical thinking is the top core skill; the tools change what the analysis is done with, not who owns the conclusion.

taskCategories.label: Customer and stakeholder interaction
taskCategories.note: Service orientation and empathy are core skills. Routine query handling is exposed; relationship and escalation work is not.

taskCategories.label: People management and coaching
taskCategories.note: Leadership and social influence, talent management, empathy: all rising or core.
taskCategories.ref: Section 3, Skills on the rise; derived category

taskCategories.label: Physical and on-site work
taskCategories.note: Care, trades, driving and frontline retail sit in the largest-growth job lists. Robotics has limited reach in most SMEs by 2030.
taskCategories.ref: Section 2, Largest growing jobs; derived category

taskCategories.label: Creative and design work
taskCategories.note: Creative thinking is a core and rising skill, while graphic designer appears among declining jobs. Concept stays human; production is exposed.

taskCategories.label: Judgment with accountability
taskCategories.note: Sign-offs, compliance calls, safeguarding, hiring decisions. The person is answerable, whatever the tool suggested.

clusters.label: Operations and general management
clusters.wefEvidence: General and Operations Managers appear in the largest-growth list; Business Services and Administration Managers appear in the largest-decline list. Growth is in roles that run the operation, not roles that administer it.

clusters.label: Administration and executive support
clusters.wefEvidence: Both roles appear in the fastest-declining and largest-decline lists.

clusters.label: Finance, bookkeeping and payroll
clusters.wefEvidence: Clerks appear in both declining lists; Accountants and Auditors appear in the largest-decline list.

clusters.label: Customer service and support
wefJobs: Client Information and Customer Service Workers
clusters.wefEvidence: Appears in the largest-decline list, while service orientation remains a top-ten core skill. Routine handling is exposed; the human service layer is valued.
typicalTasks: Inbound queries by phone, email and chat

clusters.label: Sales and account management
wefJobs: Door-to-Door Sales Workers, News and Street Vendors
clusters.wefEvidence: Shop Salespersons in the largest-growth list; Telemarketers and door-to-door sales in the fastest-declining list. Relationship selling grows, scripted outreach declines.

clusters.label: HR, learning and talent
clusters.wefEvidence: Talent management is both a core skill and a rising skill. 85 percent of employers plan to prioritise upskilling.

clusters.label: Marketing, content and design
clusters.wefEvidence: Graphic Designers appear in the fastest-declining list. Creative thinking is a core and rising skill. Production is exposed; strategy and concept are not.

clusters.label: Software, data and AI
clusters.wefEvidence: All appear in the fastest-growing list; developers also in the largest-growth list.

clusters.label: Project and programme management
clusters.wefEvidence: Project Managers appear in the largest-growth list.

clusters.label: Health and social care
clusters.wefEvidence: All three appear in the largest-growth list.

clusters.label: Teaching and training
clusters.wefEvidence: Both appear in the largest-growth list.

clusters.label: Logistics, warehousing and driving
wefJobs: Light Truck or Delivery Services Drivers
clusters.wefEvidence: Drivers appear in both growth lists; stock-keeping clerks and transport attendants in the declining lists. The moving stays human, the recording does not.

clusters.label: Retail and frontline service
clusters.wefEvidence: Salespersons and serving workers in the largest-growth list; Cashiers and Ticket Clerks top the largest-decline list.

clusters.label: Legal, claims and compliance
clusters.wefEvidence: All three appear in the fastest-declining list.

clusters.label: Senior leadership
clusters.wefEvidence: General and Operations Managers grow; Business Services and Administration Managers decline. Leadership and social influence is a top-three core skill.
